description_full: Reliance, Inc. operates as a diversified metal solutions provider and metals service center company primarily in the United States and Canada. The company distributes metal products, including alloy, aluminum, brass, copper, carbon steel, stainless steel, titanium, and other specialty steel products; and provides metals processing services to consumer products, general manufacturing, non-residential construction, transportation, aerospace, energy, electronics and semiconductor fabrication, industrial machinery, and heavy industries. It sells its products directly to original equipment manufacturers, which primarily include small machine shops and fabricators. The company was formerly known as Reliance Steel & Aluminum Co. and changed its name to Reliance, Inc. in February 2024. Reliance, Inc. was founded in 1939 and is based in Phoenix, Arizona.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 15K people. Revenue per employee of $910K ranks in the top quartile among Basic Materials peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $32K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Reliance, Inc. is a large-cap basic materials business with a $21.2B market cap on $14.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -6% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 9% cost of capital — a 9-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $502M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.12× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 18× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 59% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $9.3M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sector_tailwinds: Reinvestment rate supports 15% organic growth capacity — capital is compounding inside the business
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
31 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
